content:
Let \(C\) be a circle containing the maximum number \(m\) of birds, and let \(S\) be the set of birds on \(C\), \(T\) the birds outside \(C\).

Assume \(m\le 8\).

If \(5\le m\le 8\), choose two outside birds \(X,Y\in T\). For any three birds \(A,B,C\in S\), the 5-set \(\{X,Y,A,B,C\}\) must contain 4 concyclic birds. They cannot be three from \(S\) plus \(X\) or \(Y\), because the circle through three points of \(C\) is \(C\) itself, which does not contain \(X,Y\). So the 4 must be \(X,Y\) plus two of \(A,B,C\).

Thus for fixed \(X,Y\), every triple of \(S\) contains a pair that lies on a circle through \(X,Y\). But for fixed \(X,Y\), such pairs form a matching on \(S\): each \(P\in S\) determines at most one second intersection \(Q\) of \(C\) with the circle through \(X,Y,P\). A matching on \(m\ge 5\) points cannot meet every triple, contradiction.

If \(m=4\), then \(|T|=6\). For any \(X,Y\in T\), the same argument forces a perfect matching on the 4 points of \(S\). There are only 3 perfect matchings on 4 points. Among the \(\binom{6}{2}=15\) pairs in \(T\), some matching occurs at least 5 times. But for a fixed matching, say \(AB\mid CD\), a point \(X\) has at most one partner \(Y\), namely the second intersection of the circle through \(A,B,X\) and the circle through \(C,D,X\). Hence at most 3 disjoint pairs in \(T\) can give the same matching, contradiction.

So \(m\ge 9\).

This is attainable: put 9 birds on one circle and 1 bird outside it. Any 5 birds either include the outside bird and 4 circle birds, or are all circle birds; in either case 4 lie on the same circle.

\[
\boxed{9}
\]
